slides.text: The old treaty between Heaven and the Mortal Realm has only one clause: any deity who wishes to walk the earth in human form must surrender one mortal frailty to the Royal Exchequer every century. I am a sixty-year-old clerk with spectacles and a ledger, and once a year, the immortals line up outside my cramped office to pay their rent.

Today, the God of War slammed a bronze jar onto my desk containing his ability to sleep without nightmares. The Goddess of the Harvest paid with the ache of a bad knee before rain. Last in line was Death himself, dressed in a threadbare wool coat, who stood quietly before my inkwell with his pale hands empty.

'You are three centuries in arrears, my lord,' I said, dipping my quill. 'What vulnerability could Death possibly surrender?' He leaned across the ledger, and for the first time, I saw the exhaustion in his ancient, hollow eyes. 'Take my impartiality,' he whispered, sliding a single tear of black glass across the blotter. 'For just one day, let me grieve for the ones I have to carry.'
